title: What's the deal with the Bermuda Triangle?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the Bermuda Triangle, a loosely defined area between Miami, Bermuda and San Juan, Puerto Rico, said to have caused many ship and plane disappearances. They examine the statistics (including the Lloyd's of London figures and Gian Quasar's claims), the 1945 Flight 19 Navy bomber disappearance, the 1948 Star Tiger-era-style Milwaukee C-119 case (Flight 6-80), misattributed cases like the Mary Celeste, far-fetched theories (aliens, Atlantis and the Bimini Road, Ray Brown's crystal, Bruce Gernon's electronic fog and time tunnel, portals and blue holes), and scientific explanations (magnetic declination and the agonic line, weather and waterspouts, freak waves, deep trenches, Gulf Stream, methane hydrate eruptions). The episode closes with a listener mail about a Thomas Nast painting and a sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter and Barry Manilow
segments.summary: Hosts joke about Barry Manilow's Bermuda Triangle song and their record collections, then introduce the Bermuda Triangle as a loosely defined, unofficial geographic area and note the 1964 naming origin and Charles Berlitz's book popularizing it.

segments.title: Statistics and Lloyd's of London
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how the Bermuda Triangle debate rests on statistics. They cite Lloyd's of London figures of 428 vessels missing worldwide, which showed no higher rate in the area, and the Coast Guard's view on overdue vessels.

segments.title: Gian Quasar and disappearance data
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Gian J. Quasar, author of Into the Bermuda Triangle and administrator of a website on it, who challenges Lloyd's data and compares the area with waters off New England using NTSB data. The hosts question his methods.

segments.title: Flight 19
segments.summary: Details of Navy Flight 19, five TBF Avengers led by Lieutenant Charles C. Taylor that vanished in 1945 after a training patrol. Taylor reported faulty compasses and was lost; a rescue seaplane exploded and another was lost. The Navy first blamed pilot error, then changed the cause to unknown.

segments.title: Origin of the name and mistaken cases
segments.summary: The hosts trace the name to George Sand's 1952 Fate article and Vincent Gaddis's 1964 Argosy piece, noting the pulp fiction source. They then discuss the Mary Celeste, which is wrongly listed as a Bermuda Triangle case.

segments.title: Milwaukee C-119 Flying Boxcar disappearance
segments.summary: The 1950s disappearance of a C-119 Flying Boxcar that took off from Homestead Air Force Base for the Bahamas with an experienced crew and was never found. Only a few debris scraps were reported, possibly scuttled. The hosts compare it with the Sulfur Queen.

segments.title: Far-fetched theories: aliens, Atlantis, Bimini Road
segments.summary: The hosts review fringe explanations: UFO abductions, portals and blue holes as wormholes, and Atlantis. They discuss Edgar Cayce's Bimini Road prediction and the stone formation off Bimini, which some see as man-made and others as natural or tourist damage.

segments.title: Ray Brown's crystal and Bruce Gernon's electronic fog
segments.summary: Ray Brown claimed in 1970 to have found a mirrored underwater pyramid holding a crystal sphere, later shown at a Phoenix psychic seminar. Bruce Gernon described flying into a round cloud tunnel near Miami, with instruments spinning and a time-warp-like return. The hosts also mention an underwater urban complex off Cuba.

segments.title: Scientific explanations: magnetism, weather, and sea floor
segments.summary: The hosts explain magnetic declination and the agonic line, noting it has moved away from the area and that experienced pilots compensate for it. They cover weather such as waterspouts and freak waves, deep ocean trenches, and the Gulf Stream current.

segments.title: Methane hydrate explanation and skepticism
segments.summary: The hosts describe methane hydrate eruptions that could reduce water density and sink ships, and mention Larry Kusche's critique that many accounts repeat the same stories without investigation.

segments.title: Listener mail: Thomas Nast painting
segments.summary: Listener Evan B. writes that his mother worked for an elderly neighbor who owned a Thomas Nast painting of the head of Christ, valued around two hundred thousand dollars, which failed to sell at Skinner's auction and is going back up for auction.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts say goodbye and give contact options for the show, plus a promotion for the How Stuff Works iPhone app.
